title: Fixed point
text: Pattern fifteen: prices as doubles, or as integer ticks. Binary floating point can't store most decimal prices exactly. That costs a little speed, and a lot of correctness.

title: The general version
text: The task: apply a book update at a price, to a flat array of levels, one slot per tick. The general version keeps prices as doubles, the way they look in text. Because a double is rarely exact, it checks that the price sits on the tick grid with an epsilon, and rounds to find the level. It's careful, readable, and it looks correct.

title: Correctness first
text: Start with correctness. In binary floating point, 0.1 plus 0.2 is not 0.3, so a std::map keyed by double files them as two different levels. Adding ten one-cent steps to 100 doesn't give 100.10. Truncating 0.29 divided by 0.01 gives 28, not 29. And a million fills of three lots at one cent sum to 29,999.9999996, not 30,000. The epsilons and round calls exist to patch exactly this, and they're easy to get subtly wrong.

title: What it costs
text: Then speed. Each update divides by the tick size twice, and a double division typically has 13 to 15 cycles of latency. std::round isn't one instruction here: g++ calls the library's round function, twice per update. In total, the loop runs about 35 instructions per update, two of them calls. The integer version is ten instructions: a subtract for the level, a multiply for notional, and the adds.

title: The hot path version
text: The hot path stores prices as integer ticks. With a one-cent tick, 5012.25 becomes 501225, converted once, at the feed boundary, where the text is parsed. After that there's nothing to round: the level is price minus base. Notional is ticks times quantity, exact in a 64-bit integer, divided by a hundred only when you print it. Equality is exact, so ticks are safe as map keys and hash keys.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared 4 vCPU cloud VM, eight thousand updates into a two thousand level book, pinned to one core. The double version takes 13 nanoseconds per update. Integer ticks take 2.5, about five times faster. Most of that gap is the off-tick check: without it, the double version takes 4.5. And after those updates, the double notional is off by about three hundredths of a cent. So the speed win is real but modest per operation. The correctness win is the reason to switch.

title: The rule
text: Doubles are fine for analytics, risk and signals, where a relative error near ten to the minus sixteen doesn't matter. They're not fine where prices are compared, matched, summed into money, or used as keys. Convert at the edge, with the instrument's tick size from reference data. The rule: integer ticks inside, decimal text only at the edges.
